The Institute of Language in Education (ILE) Scheme, on the other hand, is an exemplar
of Cantonese Romanization.
It was proposed by the said institute, which had then been
a subsidiary of the colonial Education Department and was later incorporated into the Hong
Kong Institute of Education (HKIEd).
This scheme is a modification of the one proposed by
P.
C.
Yu in his book Rhyming Glossary (1971).
Same as the LSHK scheme, only 26 letters
and Arabic numerals are used for Romanization.
This system once acquired some degree
of authority through the publication of List of Cantonese Pronunciation of Commonly-used
Chinese Characters, printed by the Government Printer in 1990.
Later publications by the
administration, however, have changed to the LSHK system.
A slightly modified version
of the ILE scheme is used in The Dictionary of Standard Cantonese Pronunciation edited
by Zhan Bohui (2002).
In vowel representation, the ILE scheme renders /a/ as a in the open
syllables and as aa in the closed ones (same as the Yale Romanization).
Yu’s original scheme
has the same treatment, except that the letter a for /ɐ/ is always italicized, whereas the one
for /a/, as well as all other letters, is not.
Zhan’s modification uses aa for /a/ in all phonetic
contexts.
Finally, Sidney Lau’s Romanization is associated with a series of Cantonese textbooks
written by him and published by the Government Printer starting from 1965.
Lau has spent
years in the Hong Kong Government teaching Cantonese and was once the Principal of the
Government Language School.
One of the main characteristics of this system is that it bears
some resemblance to the English orthography.
In addition to the use of oo for /u/, it also
resorts to the use of final h to close the syllable with /ɔ, œ/ when they are not followed by
a final consonant or glide, i.
e.
goh for /kɔ/ but gong for /kɔŋ/.
Lau stated that his scheme
was an adaptation of the Meyer-Wempe system, which already included these features.
The
former two systems, Wong and ILE, adhere to the nine-tone categorization.
The Upper Dark,
Lower Dark, and Light Entering tones are numbered from 7 to 9, rather than being merged
into the non-Entering ones for tonal notation.
Sidney Lau’s Romanization, on the other hand,
adheres to the six-tone categorization.
Conclusion
In the practice of Cantonese Romanization, it is not uncommon for writers and academics
to develop a new scheme or improve on existing ones – a reason for a substantial and growing
number of systems.
The Romanization forms discussed above are those that have historical
significance and/or stimulated adoption by others who are not the inventors or definite
proponents, or their associates.
Tables 3.
4 summarize the most popular schemes over
the past half century.
Together with the Government Romanization, these Romanization forms are employed
in various occasions and reach different groups of target audience.
For instance, to trans­
literate a Cantonese term for a Hong Kong-based English bulletin, without much regard to
phonemic precision, the Government Romanization allows the largest number of locals to
understand what the transliterated term means.
English-speaking Cantonese learners are
often exposed to the Yale Romanization and might prefer a transcription in this system.
Meanwhile, Mandarin-speaking learners of Cantonese who have prior knowledge of pinyin
might find Rao’s scheme most accommodating.
In Hong Kong’s academia, the LSHK
Romanization has been becoming the de facto standard and is expected to be used by the
faculty and students alike in academic papers.
With such a diversity of uses and users of
many backgrounds, the apparent chaos of Cantonese Romanization may well be thought
of as a ‘blessing in disguise’.

3 Tone contours
The Cantonese tone system includes six or seven basic tones; some speakers
may have a seventh tone which may be another constrastive tone or a variant
of one of the other basic tones.
The number of tones actually uttered by any
given speaker far exceeds the number of basic tones; this is because the
speaker's pronunciation of a word which is carried by its fundamental
frequency is not exactly the same on every occasion that the speaker says the
word.
However, a collection of all utterances of the tones can be reduced to
the system of six or seven basic tones, each of which has its own particular
contour or acoustic shape, the linear pattern of pitch movement (or
consecutive changes in the fundamental frequency).
A tone contour has both a vertical dimension of pitch height and a
horizontal dimension of direction of pitch movement.
That is, as the speaker
of a tone language utters a particular word, the pitch on which it begins will
lie somewhere within the pitch range of the speaker's voice from low to high;
the pitch can then change by either rising from low to mid or high, remaining
level, or falling from high to low, etc.
The movement or change in the pitch
from the beginning of the tone to its endpoint is its contour.
Three pitch
levels or registers — high, mid, and low — and three directions of pitch
movement — level, rising, and falling — characterize the tone contours of
Cantonese (and some other tone languages).
It should be pointed out here
that the height and movement of a tone contour are relative and not absolute
features; a speaker with a naturally high voice (as most women) produces

any given tone on a somewhat higher pitch than a speaker with a low voice
(most men).
Listeners automatically adjust their perception of a speaker's
tones in relation to the average fundamental frequency of the speaker's voice.
It is the contours of the tones and their relative heights and distances from
each other within the overall pitch range of each speaker — rather than the
absolute fundamental frequency values of the tones — which exhibit
consistency from one speaker to another and make it possible for speakers
and listeners of the same language to understand each other.
Analysis of each
tone contour must be in relation to the entire series of tone contours which
together constitute the tone system of the language.

1 Tone contours on "live" syllables
Descriptions of the Cantonese tones customarily divide the tones into two
broad categories according to the kind of syllable on which they occur: (1)
the tones which occur on open syllables and closed syllables which aid with
one of the semivowels -w, -j-, -yor one of the nasal consonants -m, -η, -η,
on the one hand; and (2) the tones which occur on closed syllables which end
with one of the stop consonants -p, -t, and -k, on the other.
This division of
the tones by type of syllable on which they occur is related to the large
difference in duration of the tones on the two types of syllables; tones on
syllables with stop final consonants -p, -t, -k are much shorter and,
because of the final consonants, sound as though they have been abruptly
"clipped" (Lau 1977:xiv has mistakenly stated they are not really tones but
only "clipped sounds").
It is interesting and relevant to note that this same
division of tones by syllable type is made in Tai historical linguistics which
refers to the first category as "live" syllables and the second as "dead"
syllables.
This same handy terminology has been applied in the following
discussion of the Cantonese tones.
Seven tones occur on the live syllables:
The High Level tone contour occupies the top of the high register and
starts at 5 and remains fairly level or it may fall slightly toward its aid; its
Chao tone letter is represented as 155.
In general, the High Level tone is more
easily distinguished from the other two level tones; this is because its
distance from either one of them is relatively greater than the distance
between the Mid Level and Mid-Low Level tones.
The Mid Level tone contour occupies the mid register and begins at the
mid point of 3 and may remain relatively level throughout its length or
gradually fall toward its aid; its contour is represented as H33.
Perhaps
because they are the easiest to perceive and produce, the High Level and Mid
Level tones are the first tonal contrasts mastered by children acquiring
Cantonese in Hong Kong (So - Dodd 1995:483)
The Mid-Low Level tone contour occupies the low register and begins at
the mid-low point of 2 and thai gradually trails off toward its aid; but it does

context_segments.text: Implications
Many scholars contend that Chinese varieties in essence only differ in sounds and vocabulary
(Yuan et al.
Since it is easier to observe the phonetic and
lexical differences, many previous studies on Chinese dialects focus on these two aspects.
Comparatively speaking, the outcomes of syntactic variation studies are less fruitful.
On the
surface, there are more similarities than differences in the grammar of different Chinese
varieties.
However, some ‘similarities’ are in fact more apparent than real.
A number of
obvious grammatical variables have been described, but there is still plenty of room for
further research.
Given the data from Cantonese as well as other dialects, we can discover
many linguistic phenomena that are absent in Mandarin.
This allows us to have a better
understanding of Chinese as a whole.
As shown in Zhu (1980), and Cheng and Sybesma
, the comparative studies between Cantonese and Mandarin can help identify the
grammatical subtleties of one another.

2 Tone contours on "dead" syllables
Descriptions of the Cantonese tones based on their aural perception typically
state that the tone contours on the dead syllables which belong to the three
tone categories of High Stopped, Mid Stopped, and Mid-Low Stopped are
level and thus more or less the same as the High Level, Mid Level, and Mid-
Low Level tone contours on live syllables (Lau 1977:xiv; Yue-Hashimoto
However, what is really important to distinguishing these stopped
tones from each other is not so much the shape of their contours (they are not
really level but rising-falling, falling-rising, or falling, as we will discover
below), but the relative distances that separate them.
The High Stopped tone
occupies the top of the high register, the Mid Stopped tone the mid register,
and the Mid-Low Stopped tone the low register.
Tones on dead syllables with
long vowels have slightly longer durations than tones on dead syllables with
short vowels.
For simplicity, we continue to follow the tradition established
by Chao (1947:24) of representing the High Stopped, Mid Stopped, and
Mid-Low Stopped tone contours as 15, H33 (or H3 on dead syllables with
short vowels), and -122 (or -12 on dead syllables with short vowels),
respectively.

6 Conclusion to Chapter 1
In this chapter we have described the phonetic structure of the Cantonese
syllable and the distinctive characteristics of Cantonese consonants and
vowels.
We have observed that some Cantonese consonants and vowels have
similar counterparts in English and other European languages.
Cantonese
consonants contrast five places of articulation, labial, dental/alveolar, post-

alveolar/palatal, velar, and glottal, and five manners of articulation, stop,
nasal, fricative, affricate, and approximant.
The series of Cantonese stops and
affricates are distinguished by aspiration, rather than voicing as in English.
Some Cantonese vowels are similar to English vowels, but the front round
vowels of Cantonese do not correspond to any vowel in English, and we must
look to European languages to find similar vowels with which to make
comparisons.
Cantonese vowels differ not only in their quality but also in
their quantity or duration.
This chapter has concluded with a detailed
examination of literary and colloquial variation of two pairs of rimes with
short and long vowels.
In Chapter 2 we describe the system of Cantonese tones which constitutes
an additional but indispensable phonetic dimension for distinguishing words
from each other.
Tone is an inherent component of the syllable, and tonal
contrasts are just as important to the language as are the differences among
the consonants and vowels.
Chapter 2 presents both a traditional auditory
description of the tones as well as an acoustic analysis which is based on the
measurement of fundamental frequency, the acoustic correlate of tone.
With
the aid of computer software, we are able to produce on the computer screen
"pictures" of the tones which can be measured and compared.
Chapter 2's
acoustic analysis of the Cantonese tones is based upon Bauer's work with
three speakers from Hong Kong, three from Guangzhou, and one who was
bom in Macao but now resides in Hong Kong.

0 Introduction to tone
1 What is a tone language?
Cantonese is just one of the world's many so-called tone languages which use
differences in the pitch of the speaker's voice to distinguish one word from
another.
By systematically manipulating the pitch of the voice, speakers of a
tone language have at their disposal a second phonetic dimension — in
addition to the consonants and vowels — for contrasting words.
By
convention, such distinctive and indispensable pitch differences are called
tones (or more precisely, lexical tones).
The Cantonese tone system
comprises a set of six or seven phonemic tones which form an additional but
intrinsic part of Cantonese phonology.
The fact that Cantonese-speaking
children have acquired the complete inventory of tonal contrasts by two years

the tones within the phonological system.
For the Cantonese-speaker and his/her addressee the tone associated with a
word is just as necessary to its accurate pronunciation and perception as are
its consonants and vowels.

12 Conclusion to Chapter 2
This chapter has painted a detailed picture of the Cantonese tone system
which includes seven contrastive tones for Guangzhou speakers, six for most
Hong Kong speakers, and six for Macao speakers (this enumeration regards
the tone contours on dead syllables as being essentially the same as the
corresponding tone contours on live syllables but with shorter durations).
We
have approached the Cantonese tones from two avenues, the perceptual and
physical: our auditory study has described how the contrastive tones sound to
the ear, while our acoustic analysis has measured and compared their
fundamental frequencies, the physical correlate of lexical tone.
Tones in
sequence can influence each other through tonal assimilation, and we have
observed how the High Falling tone changes to High Level before another
High Falling, High Level, or High Stopped tone.
Sentence intonation also
affects lexical tone through the phenomenon of downdrift.
In some cases the
tone of a word assimilates to the High Rising tone under the influence of a
following word with a High Rising or High Stopped tone and then the word
which triggered the assimilation is dropped.
Cantonese makes use of two so-
called changed tones or pi:n-j€m for morphological purposes of word
derivation, semantic modification, etc.
We have discovered that one
interesting and important difference between the Hong Kong and Guangzhou
varieties of Cantonese lies in their tone systems: while Guangzhou speakers
12 Conclusion to Chapter 2 249
distinguish morphologically between High Level and High Falling tones,
most Hong Kong speakers use only High Level.
However, as we will see in
the next chapter, the story is rather more complicated by the fact that some
Hong Kong speakers use the two tones in free variation, while others use
High Falling before a pause that occurs at the end of a phrase or clause.
Finally, the answer to the question of the origin of the High Rising pi:n-jvm
may be found in other Yue dialects; e.
g.
, in the Bobai and Xinyi dialects the
grammatical distribution and functions of a suffix which is accompanied by
a rising pim-jvm correspond very closely to the High Rising pi:n-jem in
standard Cantonese.
Ease of articulation may underly the development of the
High Level pim-fim.
Chapter 3, Cantonese syllables and words, begins with a brief survey of
Cantonese morphology and then attempts to map out the relationship
between the Cantonese syllable and word.
Among the topics discussed in this
chapter are the following: free and bound morphemes; word categories;
auspicious and inauspicious riming word pairs; tabooed or "bad" words; the
borrowing and phonetic transformation of English words in Cantonese;
phonetic changes in the structure of Cantonese syllables in sequence in
certain types of words and phrases; phonetic variations and changes that
have occurred in Cantonese over the past 50 years and their possible
connections to other Yue dialects; Cantonese phonotactics and the labial
dissimilation constraint on the structure of syllables; and the Cantonese
syllabary in which we have distinguished four categories of syllables: (1)
syllables that correspond to the reading pronunciations of standard Chinese
characters, (2) colloquial Cantonese words and syllables, (3) English
loanwords, and (4) non-occurring syllables.

transliterated loanwords, such as /ɛp5/ ‘app’ (ep1).
Many other systems, on the other hand,
do not specify how, or if at all, these syllables should be Romanized.
For example, the use
of eu for /œ, ɵ/ in the Yale system implies that /ɛw/ does not exist; otherwise, the two
vowels will share the same grapheme eu, which is implausible.
Under the LSHK scheme,
all these rhymes are regarded as existent so that it achieves ‘phonological inclusiveness’
(Cheung 1994).
The scheme is systematic and highly inclusive, but it also risks producing
some Romanized forms unintelligible to people who are only familiar with the Government
Romanization.
Examples of this include jeon (/jɵn/) and zyu (/tsy/).
They are commonly
Romanized as yun and chu (tsu), quite dissimilar from what they are given in the LSHK
format.
The LSHK system adheres to the six-tone categorization, meaning that there is no
separate notation required for the Entering tones.
Tone number is used to mark the tones:
number 1 for /55/ (or /5/), 2 for /25/, 3 for /33/ (or /3/), 4 for /21/, 5 for /23/, and 6 for /22/
The LSHK working group decided that tone number 1 does not necessarily refer
to /55/ (Cheung 1994).
If tone /53/ exists in anyone’s speech, it is still marked by the
same number.
The use of numbering is desirable because numerals are in the basic ASCII
character set.
Since in computing Chinese characters are coded with at least one ‘non-basic’
ASCII character, like those with diacritic marks, inputting diacritics for tones might mistakenly
produce Chinese characters in the earlier versions of Chinese word-processing software.
The
ordering also reflects a more common practice at the time.
An alternative ordering puts the
Flat-Rising-Departing-Entering sequence in the first order and the Dark–Light distinction
in the second.
To write the tone number, some earlier schemes stipulate that it be written in
superscript style.
This is not required in the LSHK scheme.
Taken all together, when /jyt2 jy23/
and /kwɔŋ25 toŋ55 wa25/ ‘Cantonese’ are Romanized in the LSHK system, they become
jyut6 jyu5 and gwong2 dung1 waa2.
Often, tonal indication is omitted in translated terms,
such as the term Jyutping itself.
8 If tone number is omitted, jyut6 jyu5 and gwong2 dung1
waa2 will be expressed as Jyutjyu and Gwongdungwaa.
It is assumed that the same capital-
ization rules of the target language apply to those terms transliterated in LSHK Romanization.

context_segments.text: Cantonese Romanizaton
are given as eui and ui even though /ʮ/ is considered rounded.
/ow/ is given as ou, although
monothong /o/ is Romanized as letter u.
Thus, /sow/ is expressed as sou, but /sok/ is expressed
as suk.
The tonal representation is what gives the Yale system a distinctive hue, as it makes use
of both diacritics and letter h.
It adheres to the six-tone categorization.
In its original version,
a distinction was made between the high and high-falling tones of the Dark Flat tones, so
that /a55, a53/ are expressed as ā and à, with the vowel differently marked by macron and
grave accents.
The Dark Rising and Departing vowels are respectively marked by acute and
no accents.
Thus, /a25, a33/ are given as á and a.
With considerations of the sound change
factor (discussed above), subsequent variants may use a macron accent for all Dark Flat
tones, whereas a few publications nowadays still follow the original design and use a grave
accent.
The Light counterparts are marked with the same diacritic mark (with Light Flat tone
corresponding to the high-falling Dark Flat tone), with an h additionally attached to the
vowel.
Therefore, /a21, a23, a22/ are given as àh, áh and ah.
As it follows the six-tone
classification, a separate representation for Entering tones is unnecessary, and the three
Entering tones are treated in the same way as the non-Entering ones: /at5, at3, at2/ are
rendered as àat, aat and aaht.
The tone letter h follows the vowel but not the whole rhyme;
while /sɵʮ21/ is expressed as sèuih, /sɵn21/ is expressed as sèuhn.
Taken all together, when
/jyt2 jy23/ and /kwɔŋ25 toŋ55 wa25/ ‘Cantonese’ are Romanized in the Yale system, they
become yuht yúh and gwóng dūng wá.
Regarding the tone letter h, an additional rule was
stipulated in the original system, which states that when a syllable begins with m, n or ng,
the h will not be used as an indicator.
This is due to the fact that these syllables are seldom
expressed in the Dark tones.
/ŋɔ23/ ‘me’, for example, should be rendered as ngó rather
than as ngóh.
Most later applications disregard this rule, with the possible exceptions of the
two syllabic nasals.
The peculiarity as a result of using tone letter h causes some later versions
to discard it altogether,7 and replace the diacritics with tone number: /55/ (or /53/, /5/), /25/,
/33/ (or /3/), /21/, /23/, and /22/ (or /2/) are numbered from 1 to 6.
In this ‘simplified’
version, yuht yúh and gwóng dūng wá are given as yut6 yu5 and gwong2 dung1 wa2.
